texts.1.1: An Elegy Upon the late Learned and Laborious Servant of Christ, John Owen
texts.1.3: When such a Father doth in Israel die,
texts.1.4: Who can forbear to sound an Elegy?
texts.1.5: Which may at once His Worth and Praise rehearse,
texts.1.6: And Our great Loss lament in mournful Verse,
texts.1.7: With tributary Tears doe to His Hearse;
texts.1.8: Who was a piercing, burning, beautious Light,
texts.1.9: Whose Rays enliven'd, warm'd, and shin'd most bright!
texts.1.10: Not that this Venerable Person's Hearse
texts.1.11: Doth need (at all) the Ornament of Verse;
texts.1.12: But this Respect is paid, due by the Laws
texts.1.13: Of Gratitude; His Name asks no Applause;
texts.1.14: He rais'd Himself a Monument of His own,
texts.1.15: Which will out-last those of the hardest Stone:
texts.1.16: His Fame will live to late Posterity
texts.1.18: And various Volumes more, where we may find
texts.1.19: How in His Soul rich Gifts and Grace were joyn'd:
texts.1.20: His Learned Tongue, which living, did impart
texts.1.21: Words from His own unto His Hearers Heart,
texts.1.22: And taught those Truths, whose Worth and Excellence
texts.1.23: Were felt before in His Experience,
texts.1.24: Alas! is silenc'd now! But still his Pen
texts.1.25: Does and will preach to multitudes of Men:
texts.1.26: Such sound and weighty Doctrines does unfold,
texts.1.27: As try'd by Scripture Touch-stone, prove true Gold.
texts.1.28: Which shew the Dross, the false, the vile Opinions
texts.1.29: Of Atheists, Deists, Papists, and Arminians,
texts.1.31: This skilful Architect, who built upon
texts.1.33: Took no small Care the Diff'rence to descry
texts.1.34: Between true Grace, and meer Morality:
texts.1.35: Did not, as most, the Outside only scower,
texts.1.36: But to the form of Piety joyn'd the Power:
texts.1.37: Not only taught, but trod the Gospel Path,
texts.1.38: And both defended and adorn'd the Faith.
texts.1.39: His zealous Love to Father, Son, and Spirit,
texts.1.40: From all true Christian Hearts Esteem did merit!
texts.1.41: Where shall we find on Earth His Parallel,
texts.1.42: Who Spoke, and Wrote, and Liv'd, and Dy'd so well?
texts.1.43: Many there are that have by Him been fed,
texts.1.44: Instructed, Help'd, Rais'd, Cur'd, and Comforted:
texts.1.45: These might have made His Hearse with Tears to swim,
texts.1.46: But that their Loss prov'd greatest Gain to Him;
texts.1.47: Who long had travell'd in the Narrow way,
texts.1.48: And borne the heat and burden of the Day;
texts.1.49: Tho' to our Loss, we needs must yield, that such
texts.1.50: Should go to Rest, who bore an did so much;
texts.1.51: And may we learn of Him to conquer Death,
texts.1.52: Who, when His Work was finish'd here beneath.
texts.1.53: Lay down in Peace; and as the Sun (we say)
texts.1.54: Setting serene, foretels 'twill shine next Day;
texts.1.55: So This great Luminary's lightsom Even,
texts.1.56: Shew'd with what Splendor He now shines in Heav'n!
texts.1.57: This was printed in John Owen's Seventeen Sermons, volume 1, (printed for, and sold by William and Joseph Marshall at the Bible in Newgate-street. 1720), after the Death Sermon on Owen by David Clarkson. It is unknown if the elegy was written by Clarkson or not.
texts.1.59: In this Place sleeps One who in Grace did shine,
texts.1.60: One who Religion made His chief Design!
